title: What are packages (namespace/directory grouping), the naming convention (reversed domain: `com.company.project.module`), and how do `import`, wildcard import (`import java.util.*`), and static import (`import static java.lang.Math.PI`) work — and why is wildcard import discouraged in production code (namespace pollution, ambiguity)?
shortTitle: What are packages, the naming convention, and how do import, wildcard import, and static import work?
topicTitle: What are packages (namespace/directory grouping), the naming convention (reverse

s1_definition.profdef: A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, and it maps directly to a directory on disk. The convention is to name packages using a reversed internet domain, such as `com.company.project.module`, to guarantee global uniqueness. A single-type `import` brings one class into scope so you can use its simple name; a wildcard import such as `import java.util.*` brings every public type of a package into scope on demand; and a static import such as `import static java.lang.Math.PI` brings a static member into scope so you can use it without the class prefix. Wildcard imports are discouraged in production because they pollute the namespace and can create ambiguity when two packages contain a type with the same name.
s1_definition.analogy: A package is like a labelled department folder in the bank's filing system. Instead of throwing every form into one drawer, forms for loans go in the "loans" folder and forms for transfers go in the "transfers" folder, and the full folder path is its namespace. Naming folders by reversed domain is like prefixing every folder with the bank's registered name so National Bank of India's "accounts" folder never gets mixed up with another bank's "accounts" folder. A single-type import is asking for one specific form by name. A wildcard import is grabbing the whole drawer at once, which is convenient until two drawers both contain a form called "Date" and the clerk no longer knows which one you meant.
s1_definition.oneliner: Packages are namespaces mapped to folders, named by reversed domain for uniqueness, and wildcard imports are avoided in production because they invite name clashes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, and it maps directly to a directory on disk. The convention is to name packages using a reversed internet domain, such as `com.company.project.module`, to guarantee global uniqueness. A single-type `import` brings one class into scope so you can use its simple name; a wildcard import such as `import java.util.*` brings every public type of a package into scope on demand; and a static import such as `import static java.lang.Math.PI` brings a static member into scope so you can use it without the class prefix. Wildcard imports are discouraged in production because they pollute the namespace and can create ambiguity when two packages contain a type with the same name.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A package is like a labelled department folder in the bank's filing system. Instead of throwing every form into one drawer, forms for loans go in the "loans" folder and forms for transfers go in the "transfers" folder, and the full folder path is its namespace. Naming folders by reversed domain is like prefixing every folder with the bank's registered name so National Bank of India's "accounts" folder never gets mixed up with another bank's "accounts" folder. A single-type import is asking for one specific form by name. A wildcard import is grabbing the whole drawer at once, which is convenient until two drawers both contain a form called "Date" and the clerk no longer knows which one you meant.

**One line to remember:** Packages are namespaces mapped to folders, named by reversed domain for uniqueness, and wildcard imports are avoided in production because they invite name clashes.

sections.s2_technical:
A package is declared as the first statement of a source file, for example `package com.bank.accounts;`, and that declaration must match the folder structure, so this file lives at `com/bank/accounts`. The package becomes part of the type's fully qualified name, so the class `Account` in that package is really `com.bank.accounts.Account`. Two classes with the same simple name can coexist peacefully as long as they live in different packages, which is the entire purpose of a namespace.

The reversed-domain convention exists to avoid collisions across the whole world of Java libraries. Because National Bank of India owns a domain, prefixing every package with the reversed form guarantees our `com.bank.accounts.Account` can never clash with some other organisation's `Account`. This is why you see `com.fasterxml.jackson` or `org.springframework` rather than bare names.

A single-type import lets you refer to a class by its simple name. For example `import com.bank.accounts.Account;` means you can write `Account rajesh = new Account(...)` instead of the full path every time. Importing does not load or copy anything; it is purely a compile-time convenience that tells the compiler how to resolve the simple name.

A wildcard import such as `import com.bank.accounts.*;` makes every public type in that package resolvable by simple name. It is on demand, meaning the compiler only actually uses the types you reference, so there is no runtime cost and no performance penalty. The real objection is readability and safety. With a wildcard you cannot tell at a glance which package a given simple name comes from, and if two wildcard-imported packages both contain a type with the same name, the code fails to compile with an ambiguity error. The classic example is `java.util.Date` versus `java.sql.Date`: import both packages with wildcards and a bare `Date` becomes ambiguous. A concrete banking example is `import com.bank.accounts.*;` together with `import com.bank.reporting.*;` where both define an `Account` type, forcing you back to fully qualified names anyway.

A static import brings a static member, a field or a method, into scope so you can use it without naming its class. For example `import static java.lang.Math.max;` lets you write `max(a, b)` instead of `Math.max(a, b)`, and `import static java.math.RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN;` lets you write `amount.setScale(2, HALF_EVEN)` cleanly in financial rounding. Static imports shine for constants and utility methods you use heavily, and they are especially common in test code where `assertEquals` and `assertThrows` read better unqualified. The same caution applies: overusing static imports hides where a method or constant actually comes from, so you use them sparingly and never with a wildcard static import in production.

The senior-level guidance is simple. Prefer explicit single-type imports because they document dependencies, make name resolution obvious, and prevent surprise ambiguities when libraries evolve and add new types. Modern IDEs manage these imports automatically, so the convenience argument for wildcards has largely disappeared, and many team style guides and the Google Java Style Guide forbid wildcard imports outright.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — our codebase has grown and we now have an `Account` concept in the accounts module and a differently shaped `Account` summary in the reporting module. A developer used wildcard imports for both packages, and the build suddenly failed with an ambiguous reference the moment reporting added its `Account`. We want a demo that shows how correct package naming keeps these two types distinct and how explicit imports resolve the clash cleanly.

Problem 2 — our interest and fee math is full of `Math.max`, `BigDecimal.ROUND` style constants, and rounding modes, and the repeated class prefixes make the formulas hard to read. We want to show how a carefully chosen static import for the rounding mode and the max function makes the monthly-fee formula read almost like the business rule itself, without hiding too much.

Our runnable demo will live in package `com.bank.accounts`, define an `Account` with debit and credit, a `FeeCalculator` that uses a static-imported rounding mode and max, and a `main` that performs a transfer from Rajesh to Priya and then computes Priya's monthly maintenance fee using the cleanly imported statics. The bash section will show that the package declaration must match the folder path for compilation to succeed.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# The package declaration MUST match the folder path, or javac refuses it.
# com.bank.accounts classes live under com/bank/accounts, reporting under com/bank/reporting.
javac -d out $(find src/main/java -name "*.java")

# Run: fully qualified main class name includes its package.
java -cp out com.bank.accounts.PackageImportDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000), Priya (CUR3001, 250000), a rent amount of 50000, a fee rate of 0.0005, and a minimum fee of 100.00.

Step 1 — the compiler reads `PackageImportDemo.java`, sees `package com.bank.accounts`, and resolves the simple name `Account` to `com.bank.accounts.Account` because that is the one imported. The reporting `Account` is referred to by its fully qualified name, so there is no ambiguity.

Step 2 — the transfer runs. Rajesh is debited 50000, moving from 1000000 to 950000, and Priya is credited 50000, moving from 250000 to 300000. The success is logged.

Step 3 — the fee calculator takes Priya's new balance of 300000, multiplies by the rate 0.0005 to get 150.00, compares it with the minimum fee of 100.00, chooses the larger 150.00, and the static-imported `HALF_EVEN` rounds it to two decimal places. The clean formula produced a fee without any class prefixes cluttering the math.

Step 4 — a reporting `Account` summary is built from Priya's account id and her closing balance of 300000. This object is a completely different type from the accounts `Account`, proving two same-named classes coexist because their packages differ.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:22:30 INFO    Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS
2026-10-30 19:22:30 INFO    Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
2026-10-30 19:22:30 INFO    Priya monthly maintenance fee: 150.00
2026-10-30 19:22:30 INFO    Reporting summary for CUR3001 closing=300000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, and it maps directly onto a directory on disk, so a class declared in package com dot bank dot accounts physically lives in a folder com slash bank slash accounts. The package becomes part of a type's fully qualified name, which is how two classes that share the same simple name, such as an Account in the accounts module and an Account in the reporting module, can coexist without conflict. The naming convention is to use a reversed internet domain like com dot company dot project dot module, and the reason is global uniqueness: because the organisation owns that domain, no other library in the world will accidentally produce the same fully qualified name.

An import is purely a compile-time convenience that lets you refer to a class by its simple name instead of its full path; it does not load or copy anything. A single-type import brings in exactly one class, a wildcard import brings in every public type of a package on demand, and a static import brings in a static field or method so you can use it without its class prefix, which reads very nicely for constants, for a rounding mode like half even, or for assertions in tests.

I avoid wildcard imports in production code, and this is a point I always make clearly. There is no runtime cost to a wildcard, so the objection is not performance; it is readability and safety. With a wildcard you cannot see at a glance which package a name comes from, and if two wildcard-imported packages both define a type with the same simple name, the code fails to compile with an ambiguity error. The textbook case is java dot util dot Date versus java dot sql dot Date.

In our codebase at National Bank of India this bit us directly. We had an Account type in the accounts module and later the reporting module added its own Account summary. A file that had used wildcard imports for both packages broke the moment the second Account appeared, and the clean fix was explicit single-type imports plus using the fully qualified name for the reporting type where both were needed. Separately, I used static imports deliberately in our fee calculator so the monthly maintenance formula reads almost like the business rule, bringing in the half even rounding mode directly rather than prefixing it everywhere. The overall rule I follow and that most style guides enforce is to prefer explicit imports, because modern IDEs manage them automatically and they make every dependency visible and every name unambiguous.
